questions.qtext: The join operation can be defined as

options.text: a cartesian product of two relations followed by a selection
a union of two relations followed by cartesian product of the two relations

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 3)
Correct answer: Option A

In relational algebra, a join operation is typically implemented as a cartesian product of two relations (tables), followed by a selection
(filtering rows based on a condition). This process combines tuples from two relations based on a related attribute.

Let $\text{R}_1, \text{R}_2, \ldots, \text{R}_n$ be a decomposition of schema $\text{U}$. Let $u(\text{U)}$ be a relation, and let $r_i=\prod_{R_\text{I}}(u)$.
Which of the following is true?
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, D

Source solution 1 (score: 12)
  • Option A is True for ALL Decompositions.
  • Option B is True only for Lossless Decompositions.
  • Option C is Never True, unless it equal.
  • Option D is True for lossy Decompositions.

Definition. Formally, a decomposition $\text{D}=\left\{\text{R}_1, \text{R}_2, \ldots, \text{R}_m\right\}$ of $\text{R}$ has the lossless (non-additive) join property with respect to the set of dependencies $\text{F}$ on $\text{R}$ if, for every relation state $r$ of $\text{R}$ that satisfies $\text{F}$, the following holds, where $\ast$ is the $\textsf{NATURAL JOIN}$ of all the relations in $\text{D}: \ast\left(\pi_{\text{R}_1}(r), \ldots, \pi_{\text{R}_m}(r)\right)=r$.

Let $\text{R}$ be a relation schema and let $\text{F}$ be a set of $\text{FDs}$ over $\text{R}$. A decomposition of $\text{R}$ into two schemas with attribute sets $\text{X}$ and $\text{Y}$ is said to be a lossless-join decomposition with respect to $\mathbf{F}$ if for every instance $r$ of $\text{R}$ that satisfies the dependencies in $\text{F}, \pi_\text{X}(r) \bowtie \pi_\text{Y}(r)=r$.

This definition can easily be extended to cover a decomposition of $\text{R}$ into more than two relations. It is easy to see that $r \subseteq \pi_\text{X}(r) \bowtie \pi_\text{Y}(r)$ always holds. In general,

questions.qtext:
Consider the following database relations :
Enrolled(Student, Course): It contains the courses that each student has enrolled into,
and
ToDo(Course): It contains the courses that are required to graduate.
The instance for Enrolled relation is shown below:
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline \textbf{Student} & \textbf{Course} \\
\hline \text{Robert} & \text{Databases} \\
\text{Robert} & \text{Programming Languages} \\
\text{Susie} & \text{Databases} \\
\text{Susie} & \text{Operating Systems} \\
\text{Julie} & \text{Programming Languages} \\
\text{Julie} & \text{Machine Learning} \\
\text{Emilie} & \text{Operating Systems} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
The instance for ToDo relation is shown below:
$$
\begin{array}{|c|}
\hline \textbf{Course} \\
\hline \text{Databases} \\
\text{Programming Languages} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
We run the following SQL Query of this database :

SELECT Student FROM Enrolled
EXCEPT
SELECT Student FROM (
 SELECT Student, Course
 FROM (select Student FROM Enrolled), ToDo
 EXCEPT
 SELECT Student, Course FROM Enrolled);


How many tuples will be there in the output of this SQL Query?
questions.solution:
Answer: 1

Source solution 1 (score: 22)

The given query Finds the names of all students who can graduate (i.e., who have taken all ToDo courses).
Just by running the query for the given instances, it is easy to see that the answer we get is:
$$
\begin{array}{|c|}
\hline \textbf{Student} \\
\hline \text{Robert} \\

\hline
\end{array}
$$

NOTE that for the set union (UNION), set difference (EXCEPT), and set intersection (INTERSECT) operations of SQL, the relations resulting from these set operations are sets of tuples; that is, duplicate tuples are eliminated from the result. So, answer will be 1, Not 2.

More About the given query:
There is a relational operator that directly gives us this result. The operator is division, written $\mathrm{R} \div \mathrm{S}$.
Unfortunately, there is no direct way to express division in SQL. We can write this query, but to do so, we will have to express our query through double negation and existential quantifiers. We will produce this query in stages. Our roadmap is as follows

  1. Find all students
  2. Find all students and the courses required to graduate
  3. Find all students and the required courses that they have not taken
  4. Find all students who can not graduate
  5. Find all students who can graduate

So, that's what has been done in the given query. Hence, the answer is $1.$

questions.qtext:
Consider the relations $\mathbf{R}(\underline{\mathrm{A}}, \mathrm{B}^\ast)$ and $\mathbf{S}(\mathrm{A}^\ast, \underline{\mathrm{B}})$, where $\mathbf{R}$ has a foreign key referencing $\mathbf{S}$ via $\text{B},$ and $\mathbf{S}$ has a foreign key referencing $\mathbf{R}$ via $\text{A}.$
Which of the following is guaranteed to produce fewer than, or at most the same, number of tuples as any of the others?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 12)

Source solution 2 (score: 0)
Analysis of Relational Algebra Operations

Regarding the relations $R(\underline{A}, B^*)$ and $S(A^*, \underline{B})$ with mutual foreign key constraints:

  • Option A ($R \bowtie S$): This is a natural join on both $A$ and $B$. For a tuple to be in the result, the values for both $A$ and $B$ must match in both relations.

  • Option B ($R \cup S$): A union is only possible if the relations are union-compatible (same schema). These are not, as their primary/foreign key designations differ.

  • Option C ($R \bowtie \pi_B(S)$): This joins $R$ with the distinct values of $B$ in $S$. Since $B$ is a foreign key in $R$ referencing $S$, every tuple in $R$ must have a matching $B$ in $S$. The result size will be equal to the number of tuples in $R$.

  • Option D ($\pi_A(R) \bowtie S$): This joins the distinct values of $A$ in $R$ with $S$. Since $A$ is a foreign key in $S$ referencing $R$, every tuple in $S$ must have a matching $A$ in $R$. The result size will be equal to the number of tuples in $S$.

Conclusion: The natural join $R \bowtie S$ (Option A) is guaranteed to produce the fewest (or at most the same) number of tuples because it requires matching on two columns simultaneously, whereas the others essentially perform a semi-join that preserves the full count of one of the original tables.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Thus answer is Option A

Consider a relation $\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B})$ that contains $100$ tuples, and a relation $\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{B}$, C) that contains $80$ tuples; Make no assumptions about keys $\&$ assume that the domain of all attributes is integers. Consider the following relational algebra expression:
$$
\pi_\text{B} \text{R}-\left(\pi_\text{B} \text{R}-\pi_\text{B} \text{S}\right)
$$
Let $m$ be the minimum and $\mathrm{M}$ be the maximum number of tuples that could be in the result of the above expression, then $m+\mathrm{M}?$
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 13)

Note that for any set $X,Y;$ we have $X(X-Y) = X \cap Y.$

So, $min(|X \cap Y|) = 0$ and $max(|X \cap Y|) = min(|X|,|Y|)$

Minimum $= 0\; ($if there are no common $\text{B}$ values in $\text{R, S})$
Maximum $= \min(r, s)$ (if one relation's $\text{B}$ values are a subset of the other's, and all $\text{B}$ values are distinct)

NOTE:
If $\text{R}$ has more tuples than $\text{S}:$
In this case, the maximum number of tuples in the result of the given expression will be $|\text{S}|,$ which will happen when $\text{B(S)}$ is a subset of $\text{B(R)}$ and all $\text{B}$ values are distinct in both $\text{R, S}.$

If $\text{S}$ has more tuples than $\text{R}:$
In this case, the maximum number of tuples in the result of the given expression will be $|\text{R}|,$ which will happen when $\text{B(R)}$ is a subset of $\text{B(S)}$ and all $\text{B}$ values are distinct in both $\text{R, S}.$
